section.title: Vows and Tithes
section.sectionRationale: This closing appendix to Leviticus regulates the valuation and redemption of vows, persons, animals, houses, and land dedicated to the LORD, along with the tithe, ending the book with the reminder that what is vowed or dedicated to God is a serious, binding commitment.
section.thesis: God regulates the valuation and redemption of vows, whether of persons, animals, houses, or land, and affirms that the tithe already belongs to Him, teaching Israel that what is dedicated or vowed to the LORD is a serious, binding commitment, not a casual gesture.
section.frameNote: Four movements: valuation of persons dedicated by vow, set by age and sex, with provision for the poor; regulations for vowed or consecrated animals, clean and unclean; the valuation and redemption of consecrated houses and land; and the closing statement that the tithe belongs to the LORD and cannot be casually substituted.

units.label: The valuation of persons
units.note: by age and sex, with mercy for the poor

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say to them, ‘When someone makes a special {{nadar|vow}} to the LORD involving the value of persons,
if the valuation concerns a male from twenty to sixty years of age, then your {{erekh|valuation}} shall be fifty shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary shekel.
Or if it is a female, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels.
And if the person is from five to twenty years of age, then your valuation for the male shall be twenty shekels, and for the female ten shekels.
Now if the person is from one month to five years of age, then your valuation for the male shall be five shekels of silver, and for the female three shekels of silver.
And if the person is sixty years of age or older, then your valuation shall be fifteen shekels for the male and ten shekels for the female.
But if the one making the vow is too poor to pay the valuation, he is to present the person before the priest, who shall set the value according to what the one making the vow can afford.
If he vows an animal that may be brought as an offering to the LORD, any such animal given to the LORD shall be holy.
He must not replace it or exchange it, either good for bad or bad for good. But if he does substitute one animal for another, both that animal and its substitute will be holy.
But if the vow involves any of the unclean animals that may not be brought as an offering to the LORD, the animal must be presented before the priest.
The priest shall set its value, whether high or low; as the priest values it, the price will be set.
If, however, the owner decides to redeem the animal, he must add a fifth to its value.

media.alt: A scale weighing silver shekels against land and house
media.caption: Every vowed house or field is valued fairly by the priest, tied to the years remaining until Jubilee.

verses.text: Now if a man consecrates his house as holy to the LORD, then the priest shall value it either as good or bad. The price will stand just as the priest values it.
But if he who consecrated his house redeems it, he must add a fifth to the assessed value, and it will belong to him.
If a man consecrates to the LORD a parcel of his land, then your valuation shall be proportional to the seed required for it, fifty shekels of silver for every homer of barley seed.
If he consecrates his field during the Year of Jubilee, the price will stand according to your valuation.
But if he consecrates his field after the Jubilee, the priest is to calculate the price in proportion to the years left until the next Year of Jubilee, so that your valuation will be reduced.
And if the one who consecrated the field decides to redeem it, he must add a fifth to the assessed value, and it shall belong to him.
If, however, he does not redeem the field, or if he has sold it to another man, it may no longer be redeemed.
When the field is released in the Jubilee, it will become holy, like a field devoted to the LORD; it becomes the property of the priests.
Now if a man consecrates to the LORD a field he has purchased, which is not a part of his own property,
then the priest shall calculate for him the value up to the Year of Jubilee, and the man shall pay the assessed value on that day as a sacred offering to the LORD.
In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought, the original owner of the land.
Every valuation will be according to the sanctuary shekel, twenty gerahs to the shekel.

units.label: Firstborn, devoted things, and the tithe

verses.text: But no one may consecrate a firstborn of the livestock, because a firstborn belongs to the LORD. Whether it is an ox or a sheep, it is the LORD’s.
But if it is among the unclean animals, then he may redeem it according to your valuation and add a fifth of its value. If it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to your valuation.
Nothing that a man sets apart to the LORD from all he owns, whether a man, an animal, or his inherited land, can be sold or redeemed; everything so {{cherem|devoted}} is most holy to the LORD.
No person set apart for destruction may be ransomed; he must surely be put to death.
Thus any {{maaser|tithe}} from the land, whether from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD; it is holy to the LORD.
If a man wishes to redeem part of his tithe, he must add a fifth to its value.
Every tenth animal from the herd or flock that passes under the shepherd’s rod will be holy to the LORD.

He must not inspect whether it is good or bad, and he shall not make any substitution. But if he does make a substitution, both the animal and its substitute shall become holy; they cannot be redeemed.’”
These are the commandments that the LORD gave to Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai.

nadar.gloss: A vow, a voluntary, binding promise made to God. Because a vow was entirely voluntary to make but not voluntary to break once made, Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 warns that it is better not to vow at all than to vow and fail to pay.

erekh.gloss: Valuation, an assessed monetary worth. Used throughout this chapter for the fixed redemption price of a person, animal, house, or field dedicated to God, giving the whole chapter its traditional Hebrew name, Arakhin.

cherem.gloss: Something devoted or irrevocably set apart, often to destruction in contexts of holy war, but here of anything so completely dedicated to the LORD that it can never be sold, redeemed, or reclaimed by its former owner.

maaser.gloss: Tithe, a tenth. Unlike a vow, which was voluntary before it was made, the tithe already and inherently belongs to the LORD by definition, which is why it cannot simply be replaced with an inferior substitute.

basic.context: This closing chapter regulates the redemption price for anything vowed or dedicated to God, people, animals, houses, and land, and reaffirms that the tithe already belongs to the LORD by right, closing Leviticus with a final statement on the seriousness of vows.
basic.hermeneutics: This is old covenant civil and cultic law regulating Israel's specific vow and tithe system, tied to the sanctuary economy and the Jubilee calendar. It does not directly govern Christian giving practices today, though its underlying seriousness about promises made to God, and its provision for the poor, continue to instruct.
basic.originalLanguages: A nadar, vow, was voluntary to make but binding once spoken, requiring a fixed erekh, valuation, to redeem. Anything cherem, devoted irrevocably, could never be redeemed at all, and the ma'aser, tithe, was different still, since it already belonged to God by definition rather than by a person's own choice.
basic.typology: The provision for the poor, whose valuation the priest sets according to what they can afford, anticipates the gospel, where Christ Himself pays the redemption price for those who could never afford it. The thirty shekel valuation for a woman is echoed in Zechariah's ironic thirty pieces of silver, the price at which the true Shepherd is later betrayed.
basic.christ: Where this chapter required a person to pay their own valuation, or have it reduced according to their poverty, the gospel goes further still: Christ Himself pays the entire redemption price for people who could never afford it, not with silver but with His own precious blood, 1 Peter 1:18-19.
basic.god: God takes vows and dedicated things with total seriousness, refusing careless substitution or empty promises made to Him, yet He also builds in mercy: the poor are valued according to what they can actually pay, showing that His holiness does not exclude compassion for the genuinely unable.
basic.crossReferences: Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 warns it is better not to vow than to vow and fail to pay. Zechariah 11:12-13 records the contemptuous thirty pieces of silver paid for the true Shepherd. Matthew 27:9-10 shows this fulfilled in the price paid for Jesus' betrayal. Ephesians 2:8-9 describes salvation as an unearned gift, echoing the mercy shown to the poor in this chapter.
basic.oneStory: Leviticus closes by insisting that what is promised or dedicated to God matters and must be honored, while still making room for those who cannot pay their own way. That same tension, the seriousness of what is owed to God and mercy for those unable to pay it, is resolved completely in Christ, who pays in full what no sinner could ever afford.

context.literary:
Leviticus 26:46 reads like the end of the book: 'These are the statutes, ordinances, and laws that the LORD established.' Then chapter 27 follows, with its own closing line in verse 34. It is an appendix, and its placement is deliberate. After the blessings and curses of chapter 26, a grateful or desperate Israelite might respond by making a vow. Chapter 27 regulates that response, so that devotion stays honest and the sanctuary's dealings stay fair.

The chapter moves from what a person chooses to give to what already belongs to God. It begins with things that may be vowed or consecrated: persons, verses 2 to 8, animals, verses 9 to 13, houses, verses 14 and 15, and fields, verses 16 to 25. It then turns to three things that cannot be offered by vow because they are the LORD's already: the firstborn of livestock, verses 26 and 27, anything devoted by cherem, verses 28 and 29, and the tithe, verses 30 to 33. The word 'But' at verse 26 marks the pivot.

A few phrases recur like a refrain. 'Holy' or 'holy to the LORD' appears throughout, verses 9, 10, 14, 21, 23, 28, 30, 32 and 33. The priest's role in setting value is stressed, 'as the priest values it,' verses 12 and 14, compare verse 8. The condition for redeeming what has been given, 'add a fifth,' recurs in verses 13, 15, 19, 27 and 31. Twice the chapter forbids exchanging one animal for another, and twice it rules that if a substitution is made, 'both ... will be holy,' verses 10 and 33.

The chapter also ties back to chapter 25. The value of consecrated land is reckoned according to the years until the Jubilee, verses 17, 18 and 23, and purchased land returns to its original owner in that year, verse 24. God's calendar of release governs even the gifts people bring Him. Leviticus, which opened with voluntary offerings brought to the tent in chapter 1, closes with voluntary vows made to the LORD.
context.historical:
Vows were a normal part of Israelite piety. People made them in distress, in hope, or in gratitude, often in the form of a condition, if God will act, then I will give, as Jacob did at Bethel, Genesis 28:20-22, and Hannah at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:11. The valuations in verses 3 to 7 allowed someone who had vowed a person, himself, a child or a servant, to the LORD's service to pay its value in silver to the sanctuary instead. Since only Levites served at the tabernacle, the payment most likely stood in place of the vowed service and supported the sanctuary.

The amounts were significant. The BSB footnote puts fifty shekels at about 570 grams of silver. By comparison, thirty shekels was the compensation owed for a slave gored by an ox, Exodus 21:32, and David paid fifty shekels for Araunah's threshing floor and oxen, 2 Samuel 24:24. The valuation of a boy under five, five shekels, matches the redemption price of a firstborn son in Numbers 18:16. The figures appear to track expected labour in an agricultural economy, which is why they rise through the working years and fall again after sixty. Verse 8 provides for the poor: the priest sets a price 'according to what the one making the vow can afford.'

Fields were valued by the seed needed to sow them, fifty shekels for each homer of barley seed, verse 16, adjusted for the years remaining until the Jubilee, verse 18. The sanctuary shekel, 'twenty gerahs to the shekel,' verse 25, was a fixed standard, the same used for the census offering in Exodus 30:13, protecting worshippers from shifting weights.

The tenth animal was chosen as the flock passed 'under the shepherd's rod,' verse 32, a counting practice pictured in Jeremiah 33:13, where 'the flocks will again pass under the hands of the one who counts them.' The owner could not inspect and pick, verse 33, so the tithe was random and honest.
context.canonical:
The chapter's concern for vows runs throughout Scripture. Numbers 30:2 says a man who vows 'must not break his word,' Deuteronomy 23:21-23 warns that God 'will surely require it,' and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 adds that 'it is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it.' Proverbs 20:25 calls a rash dedication 'a trap.' The Psalms celebrate vows kept: 'I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people,' Psalm 116:14.

Narratives show vows kept well and badly. Hannah gave Samuel to the LORD 'for as long as he lives,' 1 Samuel 1:28. Jephthah's vow, Judges 11:30-31, ended in tragedy, and Saul's rash oath nearly cost Jonathan his life, 1 Samuel 14:24. Malachi condemns the man who 'vows to give' an acceptable animal and brings a defective one, Malachi 1:14, the very substitution Leviticus 27:10 forbids, and accuses Israel of robbing God 'in tithes and offerings,' Malachi 3:8.

The tithe has a long history. Abram gave Melchizedek 'a tenth of everything,' Genesis 14:20, and Jacob vowed a tenth, Genesis 28:22. Numbers 18:21 assigns tithes to the Levites, and Deuteronomy 14:22-23 describes a tithe eaten before the LORD. Hebrews 7:4 draws on Abram's tithe to show Melchizedek's greatness.

In the New Testament, Jesus warns against using vows to evade duty, as in the practice of declaring goods 'Corban,' Mark 7:11-13, and calls His disciples to such honesty that oaths are unnecessary, Matthew 5:33-37. He rebukes those who tithe herbs but neglect 'justice, mercy, and faithfulness,' Matthew 23:23. Paul himself kept a vow, Acts 18:18. The thirty pieces of silver, Zechariah 11:12-13 and Matthew 26:15, bring the valuation of persons to the passion of Christ.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to understand that words spoken to God are binding. A vow was voluntary, but once made it was 'holy,' and Israel was not to trade it down, swap it out, or quietly forget it. The rule that a substituted animal made both animals holy, verse 10, removed any incentive to cheat.

He also meant to protect worshippers from the sanctuary and the sanctuary from worshippers. Fixed valuations and a fixed shekel meant a priest could not inflate the price and a worshipper could not negotiate it down. The extra fifth on redemption, verses 13, 15, 19, 27 and 31, meant that taking back what was given cost something, so that vows were not made lightly and then undone.

And he meant them to learn that some things are the LORD's before anyone offers them. The firstborn, the devoted thing and the tithe cannot be vowed, because they already belong to Him. Generosity begins after what is owed has been given. Ending Leviticus this way reminded Israel that the whole of life, persons, flocks, houses and fields, stood under the claim of a holy God, and that devotion to Him should be real, costly and honest, yet open to the poor, verse 8.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescriptive legislation for Israel's sanctuary: fixed prices in sanctuary shekels, redemption at an added fifth, land values tied to the Jubilee, and a tithe of produce and flock for the Levites and priests. None of these mechanisms binds the church, which has no tabernacle, no Levitical priesthood and no Jubilee calendar.

What carries forward is the character of the worship it regulates. Promises to God matter, Ecclesiastes 5:4-5, and Jesus asks for a simple truthfulness that makes every word as reliable as a vow, Matthew 5:37. Giving should be honest, not a matter of offering the worst and keeping the best, Malachi 1:14. The poor are not shut out of devotion, as verse 8 makes clear and as Jesus shows in praising the widow's two coins, Luke 21:1-4. Whether the tithe is binding on Christians is debated, but the New Testament certainly calls for regular, proportionate, cheerful giving, 1 Corinthians 16:2 and 2 Corinthians 9:7, and reminds believers that they themselves belong to God, 'bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:20.

debates.question: Why does this valuation system assign different amounts to men and women, and to different ages?

views.label: Reflecting average economic labor value, not spiritual worth
views.case: Most interpreters read these figures as pragmatic valuations of expected labor and economic contribution in an ancient agrarian economy, not a statement about the intrinsic spiritual worth of a woman, child, or elderly person before God, since Genesis 1:27 affirms all humanity, male and female, made equally in God's image.

views.label: A hard text that should be held honestly alongside Scripture's affirmation of equal worth
views.case: Some caution against too quickly resolving the discomfort this text raises, since it can be misused to devalue women or the vulnerable if read carelessly, and insist Christians should let the New Testament's clear teaching on equal worth and standing in Christ, Galatians 3:28, govern how this text is read and applied today.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree this valuation system concerned redemption price for a vow, an economic and legal matter, not a divine ranking of human worth, and that Scripture elsewhere is unambiguous that men and women are equally made in God's image and equally precious to Him.

debates.question: What does verse 29 mean when it says a person 'set apart for destruction' may not be ransomed?

views.label: Persons placed under God's judicial ban
views.case: The cherem of verse 29 refers not to a private vow to kill someone but to those God Himself had placed under judgment, such as the inhabitants of a city that turned to idols, Deuteronomy 13:15, or the Canaanite cities in holy war, Joshua 6:17. Achan's fate, Joshua 7:1, shows the seriousness of that ban. Individuals could not use a vow to condemn another person, since human sacrifice is forbidden outright, Leviticus 18:21 and Deuteronomy 12:31.

views.label: A warning that bears on rash vows like Jephthah's
views.case: Some read the verse as closing a loophole: once a person was devoted to death by due process, no payment could reverse it. Jephthah's vow, Judges 11:30-31 and 39, is often read against this chapter. Verses 2 to 8 would have allowed a vowed person to be redeemed with silver, so his tragedy came not from obeying the law but from failing to know or use it, confusing a rash oath with a divine ban.

debates.bearing: The first view best fits the text and the rest of the Law, which forbids human sacrifice. The second is a sound application: Jephthah's story is a warning about rash vows made without knowledge of God's word. Neither reading allows any person to devote another to death by private decision.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 speaks of someone who 'makes a special vow,' using the verb pala, to be extraordinary or wonderful. It is the root of pele, wonder, used when the Messiah is called 'Wonderful Counselor,' Isaiah 9:6. The same construction introduces the Nazirite vow, 'if a man or woman makes a special vow,' Numbers 6:2. A vow of a person was an extraordinary act of devotion, beyond what the law required.

Two different verbs of redemption appear. Ga'al, the kinsman's verb from chapter 25, runs through verses 13, 15, 19, 20, 27, 31 and 33: the owner buys back what he himself had given. In verse 29 the verb is padah, to ransom: 'No person set apart for destruction may be ransomed.' Padah is the verb used for redeeming the firstborn son, Exodus 13:13, and for God's great promise, 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol,' Hosea 13:14. Leviticus 27:29 marks the one situation no ransom can reach, which makes Hosea's promise all the more startling.

The verb qadash in its causative form, to consecrate or make holy, is used for houses and fields, verses 14, 16 and 22. What is consecrated in this way can be redeemed. What is cherem, devoted, cannot, verse 28, because it is 'most holy to the LORD,' qodesh qodashim, the same phrase used of the Most Holy Place. The chapter distinguishes degrees of holiness: a consecrated gift could be bought back with an added fifth, but a devoted thing had passed beyond human reach.

The added fifth, chamishit, verses 13, 15, 19, 27 and 31, echoes the guilt offering of Leviticus 5:16, where one who harms a holy thing must restore it 'by adding a fifth of its value.' Redeeming a gift is not a sin, but it is treated with the same seriousness: holy things cannot be taken back at cost price.

Verses 10 and 33 use the verb mur, to exchange, and its noun temurah, substitute. The rule that a substitution makes both animals holy closes the door on swapping a good animal for a poor one after the vow. Verse 33 adds that the owner 'must not inspect whether it is good or bad,' using baqar, to examine or seek out. The tenth animal is whatever comes under the rod, and the worshipper is not allowed to pick. And the valuation itself, erkekha, 'your valuation,' carries a second person suffix that had become fixed as a technical term, used for the assessed value itself.

typology.type: The redemption price of a person vowed to the LORD, Leviticus 27:2-8
typology.fulfillment: A vowed person could be released from the LORD's claim by paying the fixed price in silver. The New Testament speaks of a greater redemption: 'it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed ... but with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. The Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The escalation is that the price is no longer set by age or sex but by the worth of God's own Son. The type falls short because silver redeemed a person from a vow; Christ redeems from sin and death, Hebrews 9:12.

typology.type: Thirty shekels, the price of a woman and of a servant, Leviticus 27:4
typology.fulfillment: Thirty shekels was the valuation of a woman of working age here and the compensation for a slave in Exodus 21:32. Zechariah was paid 'thirty pieces of silver' for his shepherding and bitterly calls it 'this magnificent price at which they valued me,' Zechariah 11:12-13. The chief priests paid Judas the same sum to hand Jesus over, Matthew 26:15, and Matthew 27:9-10 sees the prophecy fulfilled. The correspondence is ironic: the leaders valued the Lord of glory at the price of a servant. The type falls short, but in a way that honours Christ: His true worth was beyond any valuation, yet He took the form of a servant.

typology.type: The firstborn that belongs to the LORD, Leviticus 27:26
typology.fulfillment: No one could vow a firstborn, because it was already God's, Exodus 13:2. Jesus was presented in the temple as a firstborn son, 'Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord,' Luke 2:23. He is 'the firstborn over all creation,' Colossians 1:15, and 'the firstborn among many brothers,' Romans 8:29. The escalation is that the firstborn who belonged to God gave Himself for the rest of the family, so that they too become God's. The type falls short because the animal firstborn was simply claimed; Christ offered Himself freely, Ephesians 5:2.

typology.type: The poor man valued according to what he can afford, Leviticus 27:8
typology.fulfillment: The law bent toward the poor so that poverty would not bar a person from devotion. Psalm 49:7-8 admits a harder truth: 'No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God.' The gospel answers it. Christ pays what the poor could never pay, and God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The escalation is from a reduced price to no price at all for the one redeemed. The type falls short because verse 8 still required something from the poor; grace requires only faith.

study.christ:
At first glance Leviticus 27 seems an unlikely place to meet Christ. It is a chapter of prices, weights and exchanges. But the chapter's central question, what it costs to redeem a person given to God, is exactly the question the gospel answers.

In this chapter a person vowed to the LORD could be released by silver. The amount was fixed, and for the poor it could be lowered, verse 8. Yet Scripture elsewhere admits that for the deepest debt no human price suffices: 'the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice,' Psalm 49:8. The New Testament announces that the payment has been made, not in shekels but in blood. 'You were redeemed ... with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. Jesus Himself said that He came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The One who paid is also the One who set the value on His people, and He valued them at the cost of His own life.

The thirty shekels of verse 4 cast a long shadow. It was the value of a woman in her working years and the price of a slave, Exodus 21:32. When the chief priests weighed out 'thirty pieces of silver' to Judas, Matthew 26:15, they priced the Son of God as a servant. Matthew sees in it the fulfilment of Zechariah's bitter 'magnificent price,' Matthew 27:9-10. Yet the insult carried a hidden truth: Christ did take 'the form of a servant' and was 'obedient to death,' Philippians 2:8.

Verse 29 draws the one line no ransom could cross: a person devoted to destruction could not be redeemed. At the cross that line is crossed in the opposite direction. Christ, who was not under any ban, entered the place of the devoted and cursed, Galatians 3:13, so that those who were under judgment might be ransomed. Hosea's promise, 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol,' Hosea 13:14, is kept in Him.

Finally, the chapter's concern with vows points to Christ as the faithful keeper of every word. 'All the promises of God are Yes in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20. He did not substitute a lesser offering for a greater; He offered Himself, 'a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2. And He teaches His people such truthfulness that their 'Yes' needs no oath, Matthew 5:37.
study.god:
Leviticus closes with a God who takes words seriously. When a person speaks a vow to Him, He holds that person to it, not because He needs the silver but because He is truthful and wants a truthful people. 'He must not break his word,' Numbers 30:2. God's own promises are the model: He remembers His covenant, as chapter 26 has just shown, and never substitutes a lesser gift for the one He pledged.

The chapter shows that God is the rightful owner of all things. Some things belong to Him by gift, what people choose to consecrate, and some by right, the firstborn, the devoted thing and the tithe, verses 26 to 33. David confessed the same truth: 'everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You,' 1 Chronicles 29:14. Giving to God is always returning what was His.

God is also just in His dealings. He fixes prices so that neither priest nor worshipper can cheat, sets a standard shekel, verse 25, and forbids the owner to pick the best or worst of the flock, verse 33. His holiness includes fairness. He will not be manipulated by clever substitutions, verse 10, nor will He let His servants exploit worshippers. Malachi echoes His displeasure at blemished gifts: 'I am a great King ... and My name is to be feared among the nations,' Malachi 1:14.

Yet God's holiness makes room for the poor. Verse 8 is small but profound: the one too poor to pay presents himself before the priest, and the price is set 'according to what the one making the vow can afford.' God does not shut the poor out of devotion. This anticipates Jesus' praise of the widow who gave two small coins, Luke 21:1-4, and ultimately the grace by which God Himself pays the price His people cannot.

The chapter holds together God's absolute claim and His gentle mercy. Nothing devoted to Him can be taken back, verse 28, and yet He provides redemption for what may be redeemed. Worship shaped by this chapter will be honest in speech, careful in giving, humble in owning nothing outright, and grateful that the God who could claim everything has chosen instead to redeem His people at His own cost.

crossReferences.note: 'If a man makes a vow to the LORD ... he must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised.' Numbers states the principle that Leviticus 27 assumes: a vow once spoken is binding, which is why this chapter regulates how vowed persons and things may be valued and redeemed.

Hannah vows that if God gives her a son she will 'dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life.' It is exactly the kind of vow involving a person that Leviticus 27:2 regulates, and she keeps it fully rather than redeeming him with silver, 1 Samuel 1:28.

Jephthah vows that whatever comes out of his house will be offered as a burnt offering. His tragic vow stands in sharp contrast with Leviticus 27:2-8, which allowed a vowed person to be redeemed by a fixed price, and with the Law's ban on human sacrifice.

When an ox gores a servant, 'the owner must pay thirty shekels of silver to the master.' This is the same sum Leviticus 27:4 sets for a woman of working age, and it helps explain why thirty pieces of silver in Zechariah and Matthew implied the price of a servant.

The firstborn son must be redeemed at 'five shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary shekel, which is twenty gerahs.' It matches the valuation of a young boy in Leviticus 27:6 and the standard shekel of 27:25, and it explains why the firstborn cannot be vowed, 27:26.

'Cursed is the deceiver who has an acceptable male in his flock and vows to give it, but sacrifices a defective animal.' Malachi condemns precisely the substitution that Leviticus 27:10 forbids, showing that Israel had learned to cheat God in the very area this chapter guarded.

God accuses His people of robbing Him 'in tithes and offerings' and invites them to bring 'the full tithe into the storehouse.' Leviticus 27:30 had declared the tithe 'holy to the LORD'; withholding it was not stinginess but theft of what already belonged to God.

Jesus condemns declaring goods 'Corban,' devoted to God, as a way to avoid supporting one's parents. He shows how vow law, meant to honour God, could be twisted to 'nullify the word of God,' the opposite of Leviticus 27's concern for honest devotion.

Jesus rebukes those who tithe 'mint, dill, and cumin' but neglect 'justice, mercy, and faithfulness.' He affirms tithing, 'without neglecting the former,' while insisting that careful obedience to laws like Leviticus 27:30 is empty without the weightier matters of the heart.

The chief priests 'set out for him thirty pieces of silver' to betray Jesus. They priced Him at the valuation of Leviticus 27:4 and the slave compensation of Exodus 21:32, and Matthew 27:9-10 sees Zechariah 11:12-13 fulfilled in the sum.

'No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. For the redemption of his soul is costly.' The psalm names the limit of every valuation in Leviticus 27: silver can redeem a vow, but not a soul. It points to a redemption only God can provide.

Believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold ... but with the precious blood of Christ.' Peter deliberately contrasts the sanctuary silver of passages like Leviticus 27 with the infinitely greater price paid for God's people.

study.oneStory:
God made humanity in His image to belong to Him and to reflect Him in the world. Leviticus 27 closes the book with a reminder that everything, persons, animals, houses and land, stands in relation to the LORD. Some things He claims outright; others His people may give Him freely. In creation all things were His, and in worship Israel acknowledged it.

The fall brought broken words and broken promises. The serpent's first move was to twist what God had said, and ever since, human speech has been unreliable. This chapter's rules against substitution and its fixed standards of value exist because people cheat, even in worship. The history that follows bears it out: rash vows like Jephthah's, blemished sacrifices in Malachi's day, and gifts to God used as excuses in Jesus' day.

Redemption is the chapter's constant theme. A vowed person, a house, a field or an unclean firstborn could be redeemed with silver and an added fifth. Yet the chapter also marks a limit, what is devoted cannot be ransomed, and Psalm 49 admits that no one can pay a soul's ransom. The story of Scripture moves toward the One who pays that price. Christ, valued by His enemies at the price of a servant, gave Himself as a ransom for many, and by His blood purchased people from every nation. He is also the faithful keeper of every promise God has made.

The story ends with a world wholly holy to the LORD. Zechariah foresaw a day when 'every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD of Hosts,' Zechariah 14:21, when the distinction between ordinary and consecrated things would disappear because everything would be God's. In the new creation there will be no need for valuations, substitutions or tithes, because God's redeemed people will belong to Him completely, His name on their foreheads, and every word they speak will be true.

questions: This chapter insists that vows made to God are serious and binding, not casual words. Are there promises you have made to God, in prayer, at a significant moment, that you have quietly let slide?

The law made merciful room for those too poor to pay the standard valuation. Where do you need to extend that same kind of realistic, gracious accommodation to someone who is genuinely struggling, rather than holding them to a standard they cannot meet?

The tithe belonged to God by definition, not merely by voluntary choice like a vow. How does recognizing that what you have already belongs to God change the way you think about giving, time, money, or talent?

The thirty shekel valuation for a woman becomes, centuries later, the very price at which the true Shepherd is betrayed. How does seeing Christ willingly enter into that kind of contempt and low valuation deepen your sense of what He was willing to bear for you?

Leviticus closes with careful attention to the small print of vows and valuations. What does this teach you about how seriously God takes the details of your own commitments and follow-through, not just your big, sweeping intentions?

translationNotes.note: The valuations given here concern the redemption price for a vow involving a person's dedicated service, not a statement of a person's spiritual worth; they likely reflect expected economic labor value in an agrarian society.

Devoted translates cherem, a term also used elsewhere in the Old Testament for objects or people set apart for destruction in the context of holy war; here it describes something so completely dedicated to God that, unlike an ordinary vow, it can never be redeemed at any price.
The tithe is described as already belonging to the LORD, in contrast to the voluntary vows discussed earlier in the chapter, which were optional to make though binding once spoken.
